av_asset.test: Could this sound give anything away if it played at the wrong moment? It must not be able to.
examples: Echo broadcast bed — static, tuning squeal, attention chime

template.what: Each item is the brief for one blank stationery design — the paper the night prints its sealed document text onto. Documents are the puzzle payout and the biggest tell: when players crack a puzzle in the dispersed acts (solo in Act 2, in pairs in Act 4), the payout appears on their screens as your template with 40–60 sealed words overlaid, one of those words printed large, and one handwritten line in a second ink. You design the vessel blind; the seed marries it to content on party night, so every design must flatter any text. The tracker adds a done-checkbox, a notes field, and reference-image upload for your actual artwork.
syntax: One item per design. Start with the design's NAME IN CAPS and a colon, then 1–3 sentences of visual brief: 'TELEGRAM: office banner across the head, delivery stamps upper corner, gummed message strip at center.'

Every brief parks all three overlay zones and says where each sits: BODY — clean room for 40–60 printed words; EMPHASIS — one spot where a single word from the body prints oversized (a headline slot, a total box, a stamp circle); ANNOTATION — one line's space for handwriting in a second ink (a margin, the foot, slanted across a corner).

Describe the vessel, never the message: stock, borders, rules, stamps, tears, foxing, letterhead furniture. No sample body text, no sample emphasis word, no sample scribble — those are sealed, generated later, and the design must flatter ANY of them.
Fixed wording printed on the template itself (mastheads, form labels, an official stamp) must be generic world flavor that pairs with any motive — and never a word from any motive rhyme.
Legibility floor: documents show on phones. Screen any texture behind the body zone back to near-nothing; an 11-year-old and a 70-year-old must both manage it at arm's length.
Size the emphasis spot for a long word — if a twelve-letter word can't print large there, the spot is too small.
Use the notes field for decisions and to-dos ('ink pair: sepia + oxblood', 'age the paper more'); upload reference images of your actual design — one clean full view first, detail shots after.
Tick done only when the three zones' positions and sizes are locked. Sealed text is fitted to your zones — a box moved after generation is a broken document.
template.test: Could ANY 40–60 words, one oversized word, and one scribbled second-ink line drop onto this design and look like they were always there?

good.text: AUCTION CATALOGUE PAGE: heavy laid stock, lot numbers down one margin; the lot-description block holds the 40–60 words, the lot-number circle prints the emphasis word oversized, and a bidder's pencil line slants across the foot in the second ink.
good.why: Every overlay zone has a stated home, and the furniture (lot numbers, a bidder's pencil) sells the era without writing a word of content.

good.text: SÉANCE PROGRAMME: violet ink on grey stock, star-and-crescent border, a masthead of THIS EVENING'S SITTING in tall caps; the order-of-events block stays clean for the body, the headline slot above it takes the emphasis word, and one scrawled line fits beneath the border.
good.why: The only fixed wording is generic world flavor that works over any motive, and the body zone is explicitly kept clean.

good.text: LEDGER PAGE: marbled fore-edge, ruled columns screened back to a whisper beneath the body zone, a rubber-stamp box in the lower corner where the emphasis word lands in red, and one clerk's correction squeezed between rules in the second ink.
good.why: Shows the legibility rule working — background detail fades exactly where sealed text will sit — and the stamp box is sized for a word, not a letter.

bad.text: TELEGRAM: gummed strip that says 'MEET ME AT MIDNIGHT — BRING THE KEY', delivery stamps, dated header.
bad.why: The brief drafts the message. Body text, emphasis word, and annotation are sealed content generated later — a brief describes the vessel only, and inventing sample messages is exactly the habit the seal exists to break.

bad.text: MOURNING CARD: ornate engraving edge to edge, heavy black florals behind the text area, the more detail the better.
bad.why: No clean body zone reserved — 40–60 words over edge-to-edge engraving fails the phone legibility floor. Every brief must park the three overlay zones on quiet ground.

bag_item.what: The pool of ordinary objects that go into the numbered bags, the one physical part of the night. You and Susan list every item here. The game then decides which items go in which bag without either of you seeing it, and Jenna packs them to that list. Later, clues point at how an item looks, sounds, smells, feels or tastes, never at the item itself, so a clue narrows the room to two or three bags. The goal of 60 assumes about ten bags of six; the final bag count is still open.
syntax: One item per line, in the form: Item — sense: property. For example: Mint tea bag — smell: minty.
The senses are sight, sound, smell, touch and taste. Pick the one sense a clue would use for this item.
Think in near-identical pairs: two items that seem the same through that sense and are obviously different once looked at — a click pen and a dog-training clicker, a wrapped mint and a mint tea bag.
Every property must end up in two or three bags, never one, so list at least two items for every property you use.
Taste items must be sealed or wrapped and shelf-stable, and check for allergies. An eaten item destroys its own clue mid-game.
Nothing valuable, sharp, or that anyone will want back.
bag_item.test: If a clue said this item's property out loud, would it point at two or three bags and never at one person?

good.text: Dog-training clicker — sound: clicks
good.why: Pairs with a click pen, so 'I heard clicking' points at two bags, not one person.

good.text: Mint tea bag — smell: minty
good.why: Pairs with a wrapped mint: the smell is shared, and the objects are obviously different once the bag is open.

good.text: Velvet ribbon — touch: soft
good.why: Reaching in blind is the funniest channel, and plenty of other things are soft.

bad.text: Grandma's silver locket — sight: shiny
bad.why: Valuable and one of a kind. Nothing precious, and nothing so distinctive it points at one person.

bad.text: Fresh strawberry — taste: sweet
bad.why: Perishable. It spoils or gets eaten, which destroys its own clue. Taste items must be wrapped and shelf-stable.

filler.what: What an ordinary player's phone shows while the Murderer and the Ghost secretly pick an event in Acts 2, 4 and 6. Every phone lights up at the same moment, so these messages are the cover: if the innocent screens looked different, or finished faster, anyone could spot who holds a role. So each message has to take about as long as a real choice, and it has to ask the player to do something, not just read. It should still be worth having: a small nudge that helps someone play.
syntax: One message per line, then the button words, like this: <message, 2–3 sentences>. Button: <what the button says>.
The word 'Button:' appears literally. Every message needs one, because a message you only read finishes too fast and becomes a tell.
About 25–50 words before the button, so it reads as long as a real event choice.

Good kinds: a stray cat thought in that cat's voice, a nudge to look back over clues you already have, a reminder to go charm a cat, a small prompt about your bag (a sense to notice, a question to ask someone).
No facts about the case. Nothing about who, why or where: those come only from the game. A filler message is safe to show anyone, on any night, whatever happened.
Never mention roles, events, or that anything secret is happening right now.
Talk to the player as 'you'. Plain words; an 11-year-old and a 70-year-old should both get it in one read.
filler.test: Could this message appear on every phone in the room, on any night, without helping or hurting anyone's guess about the case?

good.text: Granolia is watching you from the study doorway as if you owe her a lesson. Somebody here has not spoken to her all evening. Who have you not asked a single question yet? Button: I'll go and find them
good.why: A cat thought plus a real, useful nudge, and the button makes the player do something.

good.text: Open your bag and pick out the one thing you would never want to smell twice. Keep it in mind: somebody tonight may ask about a smell. Button: Done, I've picked one
good.why: A bag prompt that says nothing about the case and fills the time naturally.

bad.text: Nothing to see here. Button: OK
bad.why: Far too short. A two-second screen next to a twenty-second choice gives the game away.

bad.text: Salem saw someone near the study at nine. Button: Noted
bad.why: That's a fact about the case. Filler never carries case information.

bad.text: The hidden players are choosing now. Sit tight. Button: OK
bad.why: Never say something secret is happening. The whole point is that nothing looks different.
